name: Saffire I–III
aka: First large-scale fires set inside a spacecraft
summary: The first large-scale fires deliberately set inside a spacecraft in orbit. They burned in an unoccupied Cygnus resupply vehicle after it had left the space station.
findings: A 94 x 40.6 cm sample of fiberglass-cotton fabric was burned twice: once with the airflow and once against it, at an average air speed of 20 cm/s.
The results were qualitatively different from Earth, where an upward-spreading flame on a sample this size accelerates and grows.
NASA noted a curious effect of chamber size on the flame.
Before these tests, spacecraft designers had to base fire safety on 1-g understanding of flame spread, detection and suppression.
meaning: Fire in space does not behave like a scaled-up Earth fire, so Earth-based safety assumptions need testing at real scale.

insight.crew: Do not assume a fire will grow and spread the way it would on Earth. In the large-scale test, spread was qualitatively different.
insight.design: Safety designs that rely on 1-g flame behavior need to be checked with tests at realistic scale.

measurements: Flame spread with and against the airflow
limits: The early flights focused on thin fuels, using a single fabric type.
The cited results are preliminary.
openQuestions: How do thicker materials burn at this scale?
Which materials that pass the standard 1-g flammability test behave differently in microgravity?

name: Saffire IV–VI
aka: Thick fuels, longer burns, exploration atmospheres
summary: Later Saffire flights burned thicker fuels for longer, in exploration atmospheres, and measured how a fire affects the spacecraft and how to recover afterwards.
findings: The temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
As on Earth, heat is not the principal hazard of a spacecraft fire. Smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern.
Measurements covered acid gases (HCl and HF), CO2, CO, O2, aerosols and heat release, and a post-fire cleanup system was tested.
The flights gave new understanding of how sample size and flow duct height affect flame spread and growth.
meaning: In a spacecraft fire, the crew's main danger is smoke and toxic gas, not heat or pressure.

insight.crew: Plan for smoke and toxic gas, not heat. CO2, CO and acid gases mattered more than temperature or pressure, so air monitoring and post-fire cleanup are key.
insight.design: Size detection and cleanup systems for gas and smoke hazards, and test the materials planned for the vehicle at scale.

fuel: PMMA, SIBAL fabric, thin cotton, Nomex
hardware: Unoccupied Cygnus resupply spacecraft, about 19 m3
measurements: Acid gases (HCl, HF), CO2, CO, O2, aerosols, heat release
limits: The published papers describe these results as preliminary.
Tests ran in an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle with a pressurized volume of about 19 m3, not in a crewed habitat.
openQuestions: How do these results scale to a lunar or Mars habitat?
Which materials planned for exploration vehicles burn worse than 1-g tests suggest?

name: FLEX
summary: Burned tiny fuel droplets in a sealed chamber on the space station to learn how much oxygen a flame needs and how to put it out.
findings: Heptane and methanol droplets were burned at oxygen levels of 10 to 40 percent and pressures of 0.7 to 3.0 atmospheres.
The tests measured the limiting oxygen index, the oxygen level below which steady burning cannot be supported. This relates directly to spacecraft fire safety.
Large heptane droplets kept burning with a cool flame after the visible flame went out.
NASA published the results of the first 284 tests for the wider research community.
meaning: A flame can look extinguished while a cool flame keeps burning, which matters for how suppression is judged.

insight.crew: A flame that looks out may still be burning as a cool flame, so confirm a fire is really out before calling it safe.
insight.design: Set suppressant and atmosphere targets from measured low-gravity oxygen limits, not Earth values.

fuel: Heptane and methanol droplets, 1.5 to 5.0 mm
hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus in the Combustion Integrated Rack
measurements: Limiting oxygen index, droplet burning and extinction
limits: The tests used liquid fuel droplets, not the solid materials found in a cabin.
The first experiments used only heptane and methanol.
openQuestions: Do cool flames matter for solid materials inside a spacecraft?
How do different suppressant mixtures change the oxygen limit?

name: BASS-II
aka: Burning and Suppression of Solids II
summary: Burned thin and thick samples of fabric and acrylic in a small wind tunnel on the space station, changing airflow speed and oxygen level to see how flames grow, spread and die out.
findings: Flames are very sensitive to airflow speed between 0 and 5 cm/s.
At airflow below 1 cm/s, flames turn dim blue and stable, but they can flare up quickly if the airflow suddenly increases.
Most tests released well under 100 watts of heat.
A published analysis of opposed-flow tests suggests flame spread can be faster, and sustained at lower oxygen (17 percent), in microgravity than in normal gravity (18 percent).
meaning: Even a dim, quiet flame in slow airflow can flare up when ventilation suddenly increases.

insight.crew: A small, dim flame in slow airflow can flare up when airflow suddenly increases, so be careful with ventilation changes during a fire.
insight.design: Treat ventilation control as a safety lever, and screen materials knowing that flames can persist at lower oxygen than on Earth.

fuel: Thin and thick flat samples, acrylic slabs, spheres and cylinders
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox with a modular fan-driven flow duct
measurements: Flame spread, flame appearance, heat release
limits: Samples were small and burned in a glovebox wind tunnel, not a full cabin.
The hardware could not raise oxygen above 22 percent.
openQuestions: Do these small-scale results hold at spacecraft scale?
How do thicker samples behave over longer burn times?

name: SoFIE-GEL
summary: Burns 4 cm acrylic spheres in the Combustion Integrated Rack to find the conditions in which a solid fuel keeps burning or goes out.
findings: The first test ran on January 13, 2023, starting at 17.5 percent oxygen in nitrogen with a 20 cm/s airflow.
Early papers describe the details of how the flame quenches or blows off.
NASA states the project aims to validate its approach to testing spaceflight materials for flammability in low gravity.
meaning: It maps when a solid fuel keeps burning or goes out as oxygen and airflow change. The record is still emerging.

insight.crew: Results are still emerging, so use this as an early guide to when solid materials keep burning or go out, not as a final rule.
insight.design: Use it to check whether Earth-based material screening tests predict low-gravity burning once the full results are published.

limits: Samples are acrylic spheres, not finished spacecraft materials.
Published results are early, and the project was scheduled to operate through February 2025.
openQuestions: How well do sphere results transfer to flat cabin materials?
Will the results confirm NASA's 1-g material screening test?

name: Confined Combustion
center: Case Western Reserve University with NASA Glenn
summary: Reused the BASS wind tunnel with narrower ducts and different wall materials to see how confinement changes flame spread over fabric and acrylic.
findings: In concurrent-flow tests on fabric, flame length and spread rate first increased and then decreased as the gap between baffles narrowed, showing an optimal gap.
Wall material mattered: spread rate was highest with polished aluminum baffles and lowest with transparent polycarbonate baffles.
In opposed-flow tests on both materials, the flame spread rate decreased as confinement increased.
NASA reports that confinement can increase or decrease solid fuel flammability depending on conditions.
meaning: Whether a fire grows or dies depends on how tightly it is enclosed, so enclosure geometry belongs in fire safety design.

insight.crew: A fire in a narrow gap or behind panels may behave differently from one in open cabin space, since enclosure changes how it grows.
insight.design: Include enclosure geometry and wall materials in fire safety design and codes, because they can strengthen or weaken a fire.

fuel: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric and 1 mm thick PMMA slab
hardware: BASS flow duct in the Microgravity Science Glovebox
measurements: Flame length and flame spread rate
limits: The tests used a thin cotton-fiberglass fabric, plus acrylic in the opposed-flow tests, in small ducts.
The steady-flame finding applies to low flow speeds, below 15 cm/s.
openQuestions: How do the effects change at higher oxygen levels or pressure?
How do real cabin gaps and cable runs compare with the test ducts?

name: BASS
summary: Burned fabrics, Nomex, Ultem and acrylic samples in a small wind tunnel inside the space station glovebox to see how airflow speed affects ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction.
findings: Samples included thin cotton-fiberglass fabrics, Nomex, Ultem and acrylic (PMMA) slabs, rods and spheres, burned in both concurrent and opposed airflow.
Airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s were used, and the effects of airflow speed on flame appearance, growth and extinction were measured.
Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 samples did not burn in space station air (21 to 22 percent oxygen) at flow speeds around 15 cm/s, similar to normal gravity. A Nomex-III sample did burn.
Together with BASS-II, it gave what NASA's paper calls the first clean and unambiguous determination of a low-speed quenching boundary for concurrent flame spread, on a cotton-fiberglass fabric.
meaning: Whether a solid material keeps burning depends on airflow as well as oxygen, so ventilation is part of fire safety.

insight.crew: Ventilation affects whether a material keeps burning, so airflow control matters alongside oxygen level.
insight.design: Screen materials by oxygen and airflow together, not by oxygen alone.

fuel: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (SIBAL), Nomex, Ultem, acrylic (PMMA) slabs, rods and spheres
hardware: Small flow duct in the Microgravity Science Glovebox
measurements: Flame appearance, growth, spread and extinction in opposed and concurrent flow
limits: Small samples in a glovebox wind tunnel, not a full cabin.
Oxygen could only be lowered through a nitrogen dilution scheme that was added in BASS-II.
NASA presentations give different oxygen ranges for these tests, so oxygen is left blank here until it is checked in PSI.
openQuestions: Do small samples in a duct predict flame spread in a full cabin?
Where is the oxygen and airflow boundary for materials planned for a Moon base atmosphere?

name: FLEX-2
program: Combustion Integrated Rack (Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus)
summary: Extended FLEX by burning free-floating liquid fuel droplets, including reference fuels and fuel mixtures, to study how fast they burn, when soot forms and how mixtures evaporate before burning.
findings: NASA describes FLEX-2 as looking at how quickly fuel droplets burn, the conditions needed for soot to form, and how mixtures of liquid fuels evaporate before burning.
NASA says understanding these processes could lead to safer spacecraft and more efficient liquid-fuel engines on Earth.
Researchers varied the inert gas around the droplet, such as carbon dioxide, helium and sometimes xenon, to see how it changes extinguishment.
The surrogate-fuel part of FLEX-2 burned droplets in room-temperature air at 1 atm, and its flame images are openly available through NASA's open data site.
meaning: The gas around a burning droplet changes how it goes out, so suppression choices need to be tested rather than assumed.

insight.crew: How a fire goes out depends on the gas around it, so extinguishing agents should be judged with microgravity data.
insight.design: Test candidate suppression gases in droplet and solid-fuel experiments before specifying them for a habitat.

fuel: n-heptane, n-decane and n-octane droplets (surrogate fuels), plus fuel mixtures
hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus in the Combustion Integrated Rack
measurements: Droplet and flame imaging, burning rate, soot formation
limits: Liquid fuel droplets only, not the solid materials found in a cabin.
Droplets burn in a still chamber with no airflow, so the results do not show flame behavior in a ventilated cabin.
Only the surrogate-fuel tests have conditions confirmed here (air at 1 atm), so oxygen and pressure are left blank until checked in PSI.
openQuestions: Do results with reference-fuel droplets transfer to solid cabin materials?
Which inert gas works best at the pressures planned for a Moon base?

name: CFI
program: Combustion Integrated Rack (Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus)
summary: Followed up the discovery of cool flames in FLEX by burning large liquid fuel droplets to study how fuel keeps burning after the visible flame goes out.
findings: In one CFI test with a 4 mm dodecane droplet, the dim blue hot flame oscillated once and went out, but the droplet kept shrinking because a cool flame kept burning.
Cool flames are much dimmer than hot flames, so in these tests you can mostly tell they are burning because the droplet keeps getting smaller.
Cool flames burn at about 600 to 1000 K, far cooler than the 1100 to 2200 K of typical hot flames.
Researchers explain that on Earth buoyancy limits how long gases stay near a burning droplet, so cool-flame chemistry does not have time to develop, while in microgravity it does.
meaning: Fuel can keep burning after the visible flame disappears, in a dim cool flame that cameras may not show.

insight.crew: In droplet tests a flame that looked out was still burning as a cool flame, so do not assume no visible flame means the fire is out until this is checked for cabin materials.
insight.design: Verification and detection procedures should not rely only on seeing a flame. Test whether sensors catch cool-flame burning.

fuel: Large liquid fuel droplets (for example a 4 mm dodecane droplet)
hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus in the Combustion Integrated Rack
measurements: Droplet and flame imaging, droplet size over time
limits: Liquid fuel droplets only, not cabin solids or gases.
Cool flames are very dim, so they were mainly detected through the shrinking droplet rather than by light.
Test conditions are not listed here yet. Check the Experiment Table on the CFI page in PSI.
openQuestions: Do cool flames occur around solid cabin materials?
Can fire detectors sense a cool flame?
